61 years ago today, the ironically-named Murder Act of 1965 is given Royal Assent, formally abolishing the death penalty in the United Kingdom for almost all crimes. Introduced by MP for Liverpool Sydney Silverman, it replaced hanging with mandatory sentences of life-imprisonment in all but 4 cases. The outstanding exceptions related to military-intelligence crimes, such as piracy with the intent to cause grievous injury, high treason, and espionage. READ more… (1965)
No executions have occurred in the United Kingdom since the Murder Act of 1965. The last were on August 13th, 1964, when Peter Allen and Gwynne Evans were hanged for murdering John Alan West during a theft four months earlier.
During the Troubles Westminster passed the Northern Ireland Constitution Act 1973, abolishing Stormont, and the Northern Ireland (Emergency Provisions) Act 1973, abolishing the death penalty for murder there. The death penalty was not fully abolished in the United Kingdom until 1998 by the Human Rights Act 1998 and the Crime and Disorder Act 1998.
735 years ago today, the Republic of Venice passed a law confining the city’s growing glassmaking industry to the island of Murano , giving birth to the tradition of Murano glass, one of the city’s most iconic characteristics. In the following century, exports began, and the island became famous, initially for glass beads and mirrors. Aventurine glass was invented on the island, and for a while Murano was the main producer of glass in Europe. Today, it’s a craft that is entering the fine art world.
From practical items like cups, bowls, lamps, and chandeliers, Murano artisans gradually began turning from applied art to fine art, with chandeliers becoming works of sculpture, and works of sculpture becoming masterpieces.
While the glass itself is delicate and dainty, a Murano glass artisan must be physically durable and resilient. Once he or she starts a piece, they cannot stop until it’s finished even if that means 16 hours of work. Neither the artisan, nor the glass can be allowed to cool down too much from the incredible heat of the furnaces, otherwise, the molten glass won’t be shapable anymore.
Murano glass artwork is now a more sensible business model for these artisans, as the high cost they merit is more flexible and can absorb higher energy prices in Europe as natural gas is needed to heat the furnaces.

items.title: Print commissioned by Nasa uncovered for exhibition
items.desc: The Pop Art at Cartwright Hall exhibition tells the story of the British International Print Biennale.
items.text:
Komtek I (left) was created in 1968 from an early computer image
A print by a Yorkshire artist commissioned by Nasa in the early days of space travel will go on show as part of a pop art exhibition.
Komtek I by Michael Fossick, who studied at Bradford School of Art, was created in 1962 to celebrate a Hong Kong company that produced microcomputers in the early days of space travel.
The print was part of a Nasa project to document the effort of sending the first humans to the moon and is on display as part of the Pop Art at Cartwright Hall exhibition.
The display tells the story of the British International Print Biennale, which took place at the Bradford gallery on 11 occasions between 1968 and 1990, and runs until March 2027.
While the exhibition also includes work by Andy Warhol and David Hockney, there is "definitely stuff that people won't have seen before", said curator Jill Iredale.
"It's a completely bizarre sort of connection somehow that an artist born in Sheffield that went to Bradford School of Art was somehow commissioned by Nasa," said Iredale.
"It was actually a screen print, but it was made from a very early computerised image," she said.
In March 1962, Nasa administrator James Webb awarded commissions to 38 artists, including Fossick, to document the space agency's achievements.
John H. Glenn became the first American to orbit the earth on 20 February 1962 and in the following decade Nasa's Mercury programme led to the Apollo missions, and eventually to Neil Armstrong setting foot on the moon in 1969.
Fossick chose to honour Komtek I, a microcomputer produced by Komtek Technologies Ltd in Hong Kong that was significant in the early years of the space programme.
He submitted the print to the First British International Print Biennale held at Cartwright Hall in 1968 where it won a prize.
Cartwright Hall is home to one of Andy Warhol's famous Marilyn prints
Created by a group of local print makers and artists, at its height the British International Print Biennale included more than 500 works selected from more than 3,000 entries.
It received work by artists such as Andy Warhol, Roy Licthenstein and David Hockney, which remain in the gallery today.
Hockney was invited to be a judge on the first biennial in 1968 and created the poster for the show, which is on display in the exhibition.

items.title: While Cleaning Out Her Aunt's Manhattan Apartment, a Woman Found a Long-Lost Georgia O'Keeffe Painting Buried Beneath Fur Coats in the Closet
items.desc: Painted in 1930, "Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I" sat in the closet for 40 years, with only a single photograph, by O'Keeffe’s husband, Alfred Stieglitz, attesting to its existence. It could fetch upwards of $3 million at auction this month
items.text:
Most people’s closets are littered with life’s spare change—broken umbrellas, unpaired socks and discarded scraps of elementary school artwork. But while cleaning out her elderly aunt’s New York City apartment, one woman made a staggering discovery in the closet. Underneath a pile of fur coats sat a Georgia O’Keeffe landscape painting that had been tucked away for four decades.
When she made the discovery, Betsy, who asked to be referred to by only her middle name, was shocked. “I thought, ‘Wow. That’s pretty wild,’” she tells the New York Post ’s Natalie O’Neill.
The 1930 painting, Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I , is thought to be the first in a series of three paintings depicting Lobo Peak in northern New Mexico. (The second is at the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the third is in a private collection.) It will hit the auction block as part of Christie’s 20th Century Evening Sale on November 17. Estimates place the piece’s value between $3 million and $5 million.
“To uncover a seminal work—representative of this 20th century master’s deep personal engagement with the landscape, a pillar of her career, which is exquisitely rendered and well preserved—is a once-in-a-lifetime moment and absolutely thrilling,” Tylee Abbott, head of American Art at Christie’s New York, says in a statement .
The artwork features warm earth tones and soft, rippling hills, an early iteration of the abstracted New Mexico landscapes she would paint throughout her career.
“O’Keeffe goes to New Mexico in 1929, and this picture is from 1930, so it’s the ground floor of her inspiration at that time,” Abbott tells CBS News ’ Noelle Lilley. “And she is very vocal about, in her writings and things, about how impactful it was on her. I think you get that in this picture.”
Betsy’s aunt, a career Foreign Service worker and world-ranked bridge master, acquired Near Abiquiu in 1963. It was a graduation gift from her parents, purchased directly from O’Keeffe’s New York dealer for $3,800, roughly $42,000 today.
She displayed the modernist piece in her New York apartment for decades. But one day in the mid-1980s, in the middle of a bridge game, she noticed a guest eyeing the painting a little too closely. Out of an abundance of caution, she hid the piece in her entry closet, carefully enclosing the 10-by-24-inch painting in its original box and tucking it behind rows of fur coats.

“I think she was fully aware of its value,” Betsy explains to the Post .

“The blast blasted blubber beyond all believable bounds.”
TV newsman Paul Linnman delivered that line from an Oregon beach in 1970. Fifty-six years later, people still repeat it to him everywhere he goes.
“It is just such a ridiculous, incredible, amazing, very human story,” director Winslow Crane-Murdoch told GNN.
That story is the subject of Oh Whale! , the latest film in GNN’s JoyDrops series.
On November 12, 1970, a massive dead whale washed ashore near Florence, Oregon. The highway department decided the best way to get rid of it was dynamite.
“That was about as bad of an idea as you can imagine it to be,” Crane-Murdoch said. A young Portland newscaster named Paul Linnman was sent to cover it, along with a cameraman named Doug Brazil. When the blast rained blubber across the beach, they ran for their lives. Their report “ended up defining his entire career and becoming one of the most viral news stories of all time.”
Crane-Murdoch, who moved to Oregon in 2017, first saw the footage on YouTube a few years later, when the station released a remastered version for the 50th anniversary. “I was quite literally blown away, to use a bad pun that we use many times in the film,” he said.
As he dug in, he found a deeper story. For years, Linnman resented being remembered for the whale over everything else he reported. Over time, he came to accept it. Oh Whale! follows that journey.
The film is being released with The New Yorker and Switchboard Magazine .
The clip has gone viral again and again for 56 years. First people requested film reels, then VHS tapes. It became one of the first email attachments and early blog videos, and then a YouTube hit.

Great Square of Pegasus’s four corners are widely visible, but its inner stars provide a useful indicator of darkness
This week, we are going to locate the Great Square of Pegasus and count stars to see how dark your sky is.
The chart shows the view looking south from London at 2000 GMT on 9 November. High in the sky is the Great Square of Pegasus, a distinctive pattern of four stars that marks the body of the mythical winged horse.
The four corner stars – Alpheratz, Scheat, Markab and Algenib – are bright enough to be visible even from suburban locations. The question is, how many stars can you see inside the square?
To do the experiment, find somewhere away from direct lighting and wait for at least 20 minutes to allow your eyes time to adjust to the darkness. No checking your phone to pass the time, as the bright screen will ruin your dark adaptation. Then look carefully inside the square and count every star that you can see with your naked eyes. Do not include the four corner stars.
If you can see just one star, your sky is relatively poor . Four stars indicate an average sky, while seven suggests good conditions. Count 13 and your sky is very good indeed. If you can see about 35, you are observing under an exceptionally dark sky.

items.text:
GNN Voices is a new series of first-person pieces from people worth listening to: practitioners, researchers, teachers, and neighbors sharing what they’ve learned and how they see things.
My dad’s name was Kiran. In Sanskrit, it means “a ray of light.”
I wrote my book, Making Sense of Purpose , in his memory. His name is in the subtitle.
My dad found a way to walk with people without carrying them; he found a way to guide them without giving them directions; he held space, he held hands, he held space for their wants, needs and expectations, and then he shined a light on what made them and mattered to them and what’s forward …
This week is Diwali, the festival of lights. This year, I want to make it a gift to everyone. A week to shine a light back on the year and move forward with purpose before we rush into the new one.
Wanting to avoid a doom scroll is hard. But giving people something to do instead maybe helps.
It happens more because of the environment we built than because of any flaw in us. We grab what fills us without considering whether it nourishes us.
A few minutes of reflection pays us back. Researchers at Harvard Business School found that new employees who spent the last 15 minutes of each training day writing and reflecting on what they’d learned performed 22.8% better on their final test.
Ten questions. Five days. One in the morning, one at night. A few minutes each. Write it down, or just reflect and take note. Either way counts.
We’re bad at knowing what will make us happy. We rarely get explicit about what made a good moment good. So we never ask people what made them happy; we ask what makes them smile as they reflect.
We are strengths to be harnessed. Not weaknesses to be fixed. And our values are who we are when the world is at its messiest. Kennon Sheldon and Andrew Elliot found that when our goals come from our values, we put in more sustained effort and are more likely to reach them.
Not every plateau needs to be broken. Self-forgiveness is the single most powerful action, wholly within your control, that allows you to empty your backpack. When we forgive ourselves, the likelihood going forward is that we’ll be faster to break free than if we carry the guilt forward. And big wins are made by small steps.
As David McRaney puts it, Anxiety = Fear + Uncertainty. Sorting what we can control, what we can influence and what is outside our control makes uncertainty feel less overwhelming. And compassion is about caring, not carrying.
Tash

The superpower battle over energy – and what it means for your bills
A gas rig in the North Sea. An oil field in Texas. A solar panel factory in China. They can feel a world away, but your energy bill says otherwise.
In January, it could jump by more than a quarter – around £460 extra a year for the typical UK household – according to the latest forecasts from the big suppliers British Gas, EDF and E.ON.
For the second time in four years, a war thousands of miles away is landing in British inboxes.
Since US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, oil and gas prices have soared.
Winter is expected to push them higher still: demand for gas is rising just as Europe's winter gas stores are at their lowest since records began in 2011.
And there's a bigger threat looming over all of this: the warming climate. Cutting carbon emissions is essential to limit future warming and avoid the most damaging effects of climate change. But keeping bills down while cutting emissions is proving hard – and not just for the UK.
As world leaders gather this week in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31, the UN climate summit, the same tension is playing out around the world. Energy and climate policy has become the front line in a contest between the world's two energy superpowers, leaving everyone else squeezed in between.
America is betting on fossil-fuel molecules: pumping record volumes of oil and gas and pressing its allies to buy them. China is betting on electrons: flooding the world with the solar panels, batteries and electric cars that can replace those fuels.
Whether the bet on fossil fuels or renewables wins will shape not just what the world pays for energy, but how fast it can cut the emissions that are heating the planet.
The UK, which already buys nearly a quarter of its imported gas from America and much of its clean energy kit from China, is being pulled both ways. So which path will it take? Is there a middle way and what will it all mean for your bills?

items.title: 'Summer was a wake-up call, winter could be dire' warning over food supplies
items.desc: Wales needs to grow more fruit and veg or it will be at the mercy of wars and climate change, says expert.
items.text:
Lydia Dibben wants more small farms around Wales growing produce
Droughts and wildfires in the summer were a wake-up call and winter flooding could leave Wales' food supply vulnerable, an expert has warned.
The country currently imports the vast majority of its fruit and vegetables, with only 6% of those served in its schools grown in Wales.
It is dependent on produce from parts of the world prone to droughts and fires, according to co-founder of an organisation aiming to address this.
Duncan Fisher is behind Our Food Trust , external , which wants to build 100 farms, producing fruit and vegetables in Wales for local markets.
Despite 90% of the country being used for agriculture , external , only about 0.1% is currently being used for horticulture , external .
Growers at Fisher's Wern Farm, near Newtown, Powys, said this must change if the country is to survive climate change, wars and other global disruptions to the supply chain.
"We are hugely dependent and these vegetables are coming from really vulnerable parts of the world like south Europe and north Africa - the areas most prone to drought, fires, and overheating," said Fisher.
Food security has become a hot topic , with Defence Secretary Wes Streeting saying in October people should have water, tinned goods, baby food, torches and mobile phone charging packs ready in case of emergency.
Fisher referenced this appeal, adding the UK "has an incredibly centralised food system with 95% of the food we eat bought from nine supermarkets".
He said: "There's no storage, it's a just-in-time system so the food is stored in lorries moving across motorways.
"That is a security hazard because it's very vulnerable to cyber attacks.
"If the system goes wrong, there's no resilience in it. The food just runs out straight away."

Fisher and Sue Holbrook launched Our Food Trust about 10 years ago with the aim of growing more produce locally for local markets.
They found one of the main barriers was stable housing for farmers.
As Fisher explained: "If there's a high wind during the night, they need to get out there and protect things.

A 1763 map of Jamaica showing the island’s parishes, settlements, and geographical features. (Photo: Thomas Craskell, Henry Moore, James Simpson, and Daniel Fournier via Library of Congress , Public Domain )
Tracing your family tree can sometimes lead to unexpected discoveries, but for descendants of enslaved people, finding information about their ancestors can be especially difficult. Ancestry is hoping to make that process a little easier with the release of nearly 4 million records documenting enslaved individuals across 20 former British colonies. They span across the Caribbean, Central and South America, the Indian Ocean, and South Africa. They include places such as Jamaica, Barbados, the Bahamas, Trinidad, Mauritius, and South Africa.
Released on September 22, 2026, the Former British Colonies Enslavement Registers collection includes around 300,000 digitized pages dating from 1813 to 1840. For the first time, the records have been fully indexed and made searchable online, giving descendants across the African diaspora a new way to explore their family histories.
“For descendants of enslaved individuals, family history research may often present a set of unique challenges to overcome, but what makes this collection so groundbreaking is its extraordinary level of detail,” says Nicka Sewell-Smith, professional genealogist and Senior Story Producer at Ancestry. “Featuring names, ages, and family connections, these registers give descendants across the diaspora a real opportunity to solve longstanding family mysteries and speak their ancestors’ names back into history.”
The proclamation of the abolition of slavery in Jamaica in Spanish Town on August 1, 1838. (Photo: Thomas Ashburton Picken via Wikimedia Commons , Public Domain )
Depending on the individual record, researchers may find names, ages, genders, family relationships, physical descriptions, births, deaths, and even information about a person’s African origins before enslavement. Details like these can be especially valuable for people trying to trace family histories that were disrupted by slavery.
The registers themselves have a much darker origin. Following Britain’s abolition of the transatlantic slave trade in 1807, the government required colonies to document enslaved populations in an effort to prevent illegal trafficking. These records were ultimately created as part of a system that treated human beings as property and kept track of enslaved populations before emancipation.

items.title: The swan sanctuary wetland fighting climate change
items.desc: The global campaign to restore the "soggy secret weapon" that can combat against climate change.
items.text:
Swans and ducks have enjoyed the wetland reserve at Slimbridge for 80 years
Most people know rainforests are vital in the fight against climate change, but now scientists say wetlands could be even more important.
Saltmarshes, mangrove swamps and wetlands can absorb carbon "four times faster than trees", according to the charity the Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust (WWT).
Celebrating 80 years since WWT's first wetland bird reserve was founded at Slimbridge, in Gloucestershire, the charity's leaders have called for one million hectares of wetlands to be restored across the world.
Sarah Fowler, CEO of WWT, said: "They are mood-boosting, flood-buffering, water-purifying, incredible habitats. But we have lost 85% of the world's wetlands."
Sir Peter Scott feeds migrating swans and geese at Slimbridge in 1947, with Desmond Hawkins, BBC features producer from Bristol
WWT now runs 10 wetland bird reserves across the UK.
Many people come to enjoy the swans, geese, flamingoes and migrating wildfowl, but do not realise how powerful these habitats can be in soaking up carbon and slowing down climate change.
So how vital are wetlands for birds, and how powerful can they be in the fight against climate change?
The swan sanctuary wetland fighting climate change
In November 1946, a naturalist called Peter Scott came to a wild marshy area on the banks of the River Severn, near Slimbridge. He was drawn by the thousands of migrating geese and swans that flew thousands of miles from the Russian Arctic to spend the winter here on the mudflats and marshes.
Captivated, Scott settled in a small cottage and later built a house right on a lake, with a huge window to watch the wildfowl.
He dug lakes and connecting channels, built hides and even towers to watch the birds without disturbing them.
Over the years, the reserve grew and became home to thousands of ducks, swans , geese as well as the migrating wildfowl.

"He really was a pioneer in conservation," said Chris Moore, a historian of Slimbridge and author of Peter Scott and the Birth of Modern Conservation.
As well as creating a safe haven for endangered species, Scott was a vigorous campaigner for nature.
He led the fight to stop commercial whaling, presented some of the BBC's first natural history programmes called live from Slimbridge, and helped set up WWF, the World Wildlife Fund.

items.title: Voyager 1 Is the Farthest Human-Made Object in the Universe—and the Spacecraft Is About to Reach One Light-Day From Earth
items.desc: The probe and its twin, Voyager 2, have been hurtling through space for almost 50 years, stretching humanity's reach into interstellar space. The upcoming milestone is a testament to scientific endeavor and ingenuity
items.text:
In 1977 , Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 launched from Cape Canaveral, Florida, with the aim of studying planets in the outer solar system. Almost half a century later, the twin spacecraft have long since achieved their original mission yet are still hurtling into the unknown. In fact, Voyager 1’s status as the farthest human-made object ever will soon be exemplified by an exceptional milestone: the probe is about to reach one light-day from Earth.
The spacecraft will achieve this astronomical record on November 18 at 5:16:07 a.m. Eastern time, at which point it will be 16.094 billion miles from our planet. That’s the distance light travels in 24 hours. (For context, it takes just over eight minutes , on average, for the sun’s light to reach Earth.)
“I just never imagined [the mission] would last that long,” Linda Spilker , a planetary scientist at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), tells Science News ’ Lisa Grossman. Spilker first joined the Voyager team just before the spacecraft launched, per the outlet, and is now the Voyager project scientist.
Voyager 1 took the famous image of Earth called Pale Blue Dot in 1990. The photo inspired astronomer Carl Sagan’s book Pale Blue Dot: A Vision of the Human Future in Space, in which he wrote, “Look at that dot. That’s here. That’s home. That’s us.”
Nothing special will happen to the spacecraft when it crosses the one-light-day boundary—the milestone is purely symbolic. And yet this symbolic event marks an extraordinary feat of science, technology and space exploration made possible by the Voyager team’s continuous problem-solving. The geriatric space probes are on their last legs, and mission scientists on Earth have had to find creative ways to preserve energy, including shutting down non-essential instruments.
When the twin spacecraft launched nearly 50 years ago, they each had ten functioning instruments. Today, Voyager 1 has only two remaining : the magnetometer, which measures magnetic fields, and the plasma wave subsystem, which detects oscillations of charged particles . In April, the team turned off the spacecraft’s low-energy charged particles experiment , which measured the solar system and galaxy’s electrons, ions and cosmic rays. items.text:
Installation view, Yoshitomo Nara, David Zwirner, New York, November 5—December 12, 2026.
Japanese artist Yoshitomo Nara is bringing his instantly recognizable characters back to New York with a major exhibition at David Zwirner. Spanning two of the gallery’s Chelsea locations, the presentation features nearly 100 works, including new paintings, drawings, recent sculptures, and selections from earlier decades. It marks Nara’s first solo exhibition with David Zwirner and his first major solo presentation in New York in nearly a decade.
Best known for his oversized, wide-eyed figures, Nara has developed a visual language that balances playful imagery with a rebellious edge. His young-looking subjects often appear innocent at first glance, but their expressions suggest something more complicated. Some stare directly at the viewer with quiet defiance, while others carry an unmistakable sense of melancholy. Beneath their cartoonlike appearance, Nara’s characters confront ideas about childhood, vulnerability, resistance, and the realities of the world around them.
The exhibition also traces the development of Nara’s distinctive style. Earlier works from the late 1980s and 1990s appear alongside new pieces, offering a closer look at how his imagery has evolved. His latest paintings introduce muted colors and layered surfaces, while large-scale monochromatic drawings made with industrial paint sticks reveal the expressive energy of his drawing practice.
At the gallery’s 19th Street location, 13 monumental bronze sculptures transform the space. Coated in matte white, the oversized heads recall the snow-covered forests near Mount Hakkōda in northern Japan, where Nara grew up. Their imposing scale contrasts with their softly illuminated surfaces, creating an atmosphere of stillness. Together, the sculptures connect his familiar characters to the natural landscapes and childhood memories that continue to inform his work.

items.title: Four grizzly bears killed in Canada after fatal attack on mother and daughter
items.desc: The sow and her three cubs were responsible for killing Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20, earlier this month.
items.text:
Between 10,000 and 13,000 grizzly bears are estimated to live in British Columbia (file image)
Four grizzly bears have been killed in connection with a fatal attack on a mother and daughter in the Canadian province of British Columbia.
Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20, died earlier this month after going on an afternoon walk in a trail area in Bella Coola.
The British Columbia Conservation Office Service (BCCOS) launched an investigation into their deaths and forensic testing has since confirmed a sow and her three cubs were responsible for the attack.
All four were destroyed "in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines" to protect the public, BCCOS Inspector Jeff Tyre said in an update on Tuesday.
Mother and daughter die after suspected grizzly bear attack in Canada
"Evidence from the investigation as well as animal DNA was analysed and conclusively linked to a sow and its three offspring," he added.
The attack "likely involved predatory behaviour", which Tyre said was "very rare".
He added that more than a dozen conservation officers took part in the investigation over the past week, amid "difficult terrain and weather".
Balcarras and Reed were "two peas in a pod" who "got along really, really well" and shared many hobbies, Balcarras' brother, Josh, told CBC.
"When Jenny hiked, Selah was right there beside her," he said.
Tyre said DNA testing also confirmed the four bears were not involved in a 2025 attack on a school group also in the Bella Coola area.
The incident in November of last year saw 11 people injured, two of them critically, while the bear responsible was never found.
"Today, we have learned from the BC Conservation Officer Service members that they have captured and euthanized the bears involved in the recent fatal attack," said Samuel Schooner, Elected Chief of the Nuxalk Nation, in a statement.
"We would like to thank the BC Conservation Officer Service for their dedication and hard work to resolve this incident. This attack has been deeply re-triggering for our community members as we continue to recover from last year's attack. Our thoughts remain with the victims' families."

items.title: A Rare Surviving Letter From Martha Washington Sheds Light on Her Young Daughter's Struggle With Epilepsy
items.desc: Recently obtained by the Library of Congress, the 1760 letter offers positive news about the health of four-year-old Martha Parke Custis, known as Patsy, the stepdaughter of George Washington
items.text:
More than 260 years ago, Martha Washington wrote to a friend with encouraging news about her young daughter’s health. Now, that letter has found a new home at the Library of Congress, offering a rare glimpse into the family’s private life.
Martha penned the note on September 29, 1760. Writing to Margaret Bolan Green, she provided an update on her four-year-old daughter “Patsy.”
“I have the pleasure to tell you my dear little girl is much better,” she wrote. “She has lost her fitts & fevours bout and seems to be getting well very fast.”
The Library of Congress purchased the letter for $47,500 in June during a Heritage Auctions sale, with funding from the James Madison Council’s Edwin L. Cox Legacy Trust, a permanent endowment that helps the library acquire materials. The library already had 11 of Martha’s letters, but this is the first that bears her handwriting.
“Very few of Martha Washington’s letters survive, as she appears to have destroyed most of her own private correspondence,” Elizabeth Novara , the American women’s history specialist for the library’s Manuscript Division, writes in a blog post . “Even brief documentation of her relationships with family and friends, as may be found in this letter, is important to understanding women’s lives during this time period.”
“Patsy”—whose full name was Martha Parke Custis —was one of the four children Martha had with her first husband, Daniel Parke Custis . The two had been married for just seven years when Custis died from a sudden illness in July 1757, at the age of 45. Two years later, at age 27, the widowed Martha married George Washington. Together, they raised the two surviving children from Martha’s first marriage, Patsy and John “Jacky” Parke Custis . (The other two, Daniel Parke Custis and Frances Parke Custis, died while their father was still alive.).
Historians believe that William Costin , a prominent member of Washington, D.C.’s free Black community, was likely Martha Washington’s grandson —the child of her son from her first marriage, Jacky, and an enslaved woman.
Martha wrote the letter after George Washington had served as commander of the Virginia Regiment during the French and Indian War but before he had become the nation’s first president . Historians now suspect that Patsy’s “fitts & fevours” were symptoms of epilepsy , a neurological disorder caused by abnormal bursts of electrical activity in the brain. items.desc: Hubs offering training in conservation work are to be set up in Torridon, Morvern and mid-Argyll.
items.text:
Torridon is one of three areas where the Our Rainforest Futures project aims to restore woodlands
Almost £6m has been given to a five-year project set up to restore Scotland's rare rainforest.
The award from the National Lottery Heritage Fund will support the creation of three hubs to be located in Torridon, Morvern and mid-Argyll.
Through the Our Rainforest Futures project local people will be given training and work opportunities around habitat restoration, deer management and the removal of invasive species.
About 75,000 acres (30,351ha) of rain-soaked woodlands on the west coast are designated Atlantic rainforest because of the rare oceanic plant life.
Rare species found in Scotland's declining rainforest
When Amazon leaders blessed Scotland's rainforest
The forest has been found to be home to hundreds of species including glow worms, slime moulds and rare lichens.
Overgrazing by deer and livestock, invasive plant species and disease are among the threats to the surviving areas of woodland.
The Torridon hub would involve communities in Kinlochewe, Shieldaig, Lochcarron, Applecross and Gairloch.
In Morvern, the project would include Lochaline, Strontian and Tobermory in Mull.
Mid-Argyll's hub would involve communities Crinan, Tayvallich, Lochgilphead, Ardrishaig and Tarbert.
Tobermory on Mull is among communities that will be asked to be involved in mid-Argyll
Our Rainforest Futures is an Alliance for Scotland's Rainforest project led by the Woodland Trust Scotland.
Argyll Countryside Trust, Community Woodlands Association, Plantlife, RSPB Scotland and SRUC are involved.
Caroline Clark, Scotland director of The National Lottery Heritage Fund, said Scotland's rainforest was internationally significant but largely unknown.
She said: "A 2025 survey found fewer than one in three people even know it exists.
"This major investment, using funds raised by National Lottery players, recognises that the future of our rainforest and the future of many west coast communities are closely linked. With the right support, both can thrive."
Julie Stoneman, Saving Scotland's Rainforest Programme manager at the charity Plantlife, said it was hoped the project could create more than 20 jobs and 15 trainee posts.

Mosquitos may be small, but they are one of the biggest annoyances out there. Many scientists and developers have devoted years to research ways to get rid of the annoying bugs, resulting in many approaches from plant-based traps to lab-raised sterilizing mosquitoes . Now, a Chinese start-up has turned to AI-powered cameras and lasers to eliminate the pesky insects. Called Photon Matrix , this device is described as the world’s first portable laser mosquito air defense.
Photon Matrix uses the same LiDar technology found in self-driving cars to scan the area, measure distance, and lock the mosquito’s position. Based on the returned data, the internal laser directs the beam to the target position. The laser then destroys the wings of the mosquito in one precise zap. Photon Matrix says there is no smoke or burning smell following the operation.
“When a mosquito appears, the system detects the change in distance and confirms its size,” the company explains. “Only when the target matches the characteristics of a mosquito will it fire a high-power laser along the same optical path to disable the wings. If the background is beyond the effective range or no solid background is detected, the laser is automatically disabled to ensure safety.”
Photon Matrix has two versions: one for outdoors and one for indoors. The first features a visible blue flash when the laser is shot, allowing users to see the system in action, making it better for yards, patios, and campsites. The latter works with infrared light, making it invisible to the human eyes, offering a more discreet operation in bedrooms and living rooms. The company says there is no difference in their performance.
The promising concept of a tech-forward solution that can end mosquitos without chemicals and harmful residues made Photon Matrix a massive success on Indiegogo , where it raised HK$22,674,574 (approximately US$2,890,089). The company has also said that they received 5,000 prepaid orders, with the initial monthly production of Photon Matrix being between 3,000 and 5,000 units.

A ban on industrial scallop dredging has been “the most amazing thing to happen” to the residents, both man and marine, of the Summer Isles.
In place for 10 years, the ban has protected this extraordinary kind of magenta-colored seaweed called maerl, which forms hard, chalky nodules like coral on the seabed, and has allowed for whales, dolphins, porpoises, and key fish stocks to thrive.
Scallop dredging around the Summer Isles had damaged this incredible marine seascape for decades until a coalition of citizen scientists and activists got the activity banned inside a 150,000-acre protected area off the northwest coast of Scotland that contains all the area’s maerl beds, including 2 that are over a mile long which have been growing in the same place for 9,000 years.
Maerl builds up overtime into beds and carpets that interlock, creating magnificent marine habitat for fish species to breed.
Looking somewhat like the pieces from a game of knucklebones, the free movement of water between each nodule provides for excellent circulation which the foundational species of the marine food web need. They in turn provide for the species above and beyond them, all the way up to dolphins and humans.
The protections have been the “most amazing thing to happen to the Summer Isles,” one local activist and artist named Diyanna Ross told the Guardian. “It is an archipelago that is made in heaven for breeding fish.”
The Blue Hope Alliance, of which Ross is a part, also includes an association of Scottish “creel” fishermen, a smaller, more sustainable method of harvesting seafood that doesn’t deplete underlying stocks.
Decades of dredging had severely depleted scallop numbers, requiring industrial fishing operations to damage more and more seabed in search of the bivalves.
The 10-year-old campaign to ban scallop dredging, the Guardian reports , was as much about allowing these creel fishermen to continue to harvest scallops as it was about allowing the scallop to recover.

items.desc: Satellite data suggests water in and around the huge area filled with human-made debris has become more blue-green over the past two decades. Computer simulations suggest microplastics are to blame, but researchers need samples to confirm their hypothesis
items.text:
Out in the Pacific Ocean, halfway between California and Hawaii, lies a massive collection of human-made debris that spans an area roughly twice the size of Texas . Known as the Great Pacific Garbage Patch, its accumulation of microplastics has now grown so large that it seems to be changing the color of the ocean.
Twenty years of satellite data suggests that the water in and around the trash pile has become more blue-green. Though the researchers couldn’t confirm microplastics are behind the color shift, computer simulations hint that that is likely the case. The findings, published in the journal Communications Earth & Environment on November 5, could help experts identify the most heavily polluted areas of the ocean to guide cleanup efforts.
“It’s shocking and worrying,” says Aron Stubbins , a chemist and co-director of Northeastern University’s Plastics Center who wasn’t involved in the work, to Evan Bush at NBC News . “The fact that we can see plastics from space is concerning, as well as that there’s enough plastic out there that it’s changing the optical signal of the ocean, because that means it’s altering the light field in the ocean and potentially the way the ocean warms and cools.”
The color of the ocean reflects whatever is in its upper layer. That’s why it’s usually blue ; water absorbs longer, redder wavelengths of light and scatters shorter, bluer wavelengths. Other elements, like sediment and microscopic organisms called phytoplankton, can affect the ocean’s hue, since sunlight interacts with those objects differently. From the brink of extinction to roaming across 6,500 square miles, populations of Cantabrian brown bears have doubled in Spain over the last 20 years to 370.
Numbering as few as 140 by estimates in the early 21st century, they’re another example of Spain’s ongoing success in protecting several of the country’s endemic species.
Taking its name from the far northern Spanish region whose mountains stand as the bear’s last redoubt, Cantabrian brown bears can actually be found across the regions of Asturians, Leon, Galicia, and Palencia, in addition to Cantabria.
By restricting the movement of animals, the Iberian Peninsula’s northern mountain ranges have led to high rates of endemism in Spain and Portugal among animals such as the wolf, lynx, and bear.
Direct human persecution and the conversion of wilderness to agricultural land gradually impacted the brown bear’s numbers until they could only be found in Cantabria. Yet they clung to existence in the mountains until sufficient protections were put in place for them to gain a second wind.
A study published in 2023 bears witness to the successful survival and spread by Spain’s bears. Published in the journal Conservation Science and Practice, it found that the government’s continual protection measures and establishment of new protected areas, coupled with rural depopulation, allowed the bears to substantially recover.
Using all data available to them, the authors measured the changes in population numbers across 3 periods: from 1982 to 1992, from 1993 to 2002, and from 2003 to 2012.
While a 25% reduction in the numbers of bears was observed between the first 2 periods, this was followed by a 70% increase by the end of the 3rd period. That final period also saw their breeding ranges expand by 30%, such that Cantabria’s 2 breeding populations now overlap, having been separated for decades by an 18-24 mile series of gorges with a highway running through them.
The first 2 periods coincided with the creation of Somiedo Natural Park and Redes National Park respectively, which increased the amount of protected areas centered on the last remaining populations of brown bears 688 square kilometers. Fines for unauthorized killing of bears reached some $350,000.
Additional growth in the geographical range of 77% was observed by the authors between 2013 and 2022 in exactly the proportion and areas they predicted.

The city of Baku, Azerbaijan, recently finished hosting a festival showcasing its heritage alongside local and international artists. The second annual Fly to Baku. Art Weekend concluded on November 1, 2026, highlighting the city’s culture. This included over 30 of Baku’s museums, galleries, palaces, and cultural institutions. The incredible Zaha Hadid-designed Heydar Aliyev Center served as one of the weekend’s main venues.
Baku transformed during the art weekend, utilizing the city as an open-air stage for art and design. In its second year, the event featured several high-profile creatives. items.title: This Adorable, Orphaned Baby Walrus Was Rescued by Two Researchers in Alaska. Now, He's Found a New Home in Florida
items.desc: The scientists were conducting fieldwork on a remote beach in northwestern Alaska when they spotted the roughly 5-month-old calf. The little one, named Annautaq, will not be able to return to the wild because he requires constant human care and will become too habituated to people
items.text:
A baby walrus left an orphan in Alaska has found a permanent home at SeaWorld Orlando after a days-long rescue mission and extensive rehabilitation period.
On September 11, college student Violet Anniskett was conducting research on a remote beach in northwestern Alaska when she saw something completely unexpected between a pair of adult walrus carcasses: a lone calf, alive.
“I was in shock,” she tells Ishani Desai at the New York Times . As part of an internship, she had been surveying the beach with Tony Fischbach , a wildlife biologist with the U.S. Geological Survey. The duo was looking for fresh Pacific walrus carcasses that they could sample to test for algal toxins to better understand the animals’ baseline levels.
The researchers quickly requested approval from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) and the local Inupiaq community, which Anniskett is a member of, to rehabilitate the roughly 5-month-old male calf. They named him Annautaq (pronounced “ah-NOW-tuq”), after Anniskett’s father.
“It’s a big part of our culture that we harvest animals for subsistence living,” she tells Casey Grove at Alaska Public Media . “It was very important for us to ask the community first, and as soon as they decided as a whole, then we’re able to move forward with the steps of saving him through the SeaLife Center.”
Still, there were many steps to come. After receiving the proper permissions, the approximately 185-pound calf had to get to the Alaska SeaLife Center, the state’s only permanent marine mammal rehabilitation facility, more than 800 miles away in the southern city of Seward. Stormy weather conditions meant that they couldn’t move the hefty little walrus for days, leaving the two researchers to care for Annautaq on their own as predators loomed.
“When we found him, a determined flock of gulls was intent on scavenging him. He was in immediate peril of suffering this fate had we not gotten approval to intervene. Two polar bears were also active on the island,” Fischbach says in a statement .
The two researchers guided Annautaq to an abandoned building that could shelter him from hungry onlookers and stayed there with him for nearly four days. Walrus calves rely solely on their mother’s milk, but Anniskett and Fischbach didn’t have any formula on hand. So, they fed him a mixture of honey and water, reports the Times .
Adult male Pacific walruses can grow to up to 12 feet long and weigh up to two tons .

The painting, which Lambert created at University College London (UCL), follows its new report, which outlines the importance of healthy soils and steps for their restoration.

Through his work with scientists, Lambert said he had been taught about the "perils and the needs of soil".

Combining body mass index with other measurements and tests would lead to better care and outcomes, experts say
An alternative to BMI for diagnosing obesity could prevent misdiagnosis in millions of people worldwide, according to doctors who found it more accurately distinguished healthy people from those with harmful excess body fat.
Medical experts have long considered body mass index a blunt instrument for defining obesity, leading to concerns that substantial numbers of people with excess body fat are missed while others who are healthy are wrongly diagnosed.
The new approach, which combines BMI with other body measurements and organ function tests, suggests BMI alone misses obesity in 5-9% of adults, while wrongly diagnosing the condition in as many as 3%.
“This misclassification can account for tens of millions of people, so the inaccuracy of BMI is a big problem at scale and also for individuals,” said Francisco Rubino, a professor of metabolic and bariatric surgery at King’s College London.
BMI is calculated by dividing weight in kilograms by height in metres squared. About 1.6 billion people worldwide are classified as overweight, meaning their BMI falls between 25 and 29.9, and nearly a billion with a BMI of 30 or more are considered obese. Two-thirds of adults in the UK and more than 70% of adults in the US are overweight or obese based on BMI alone.
Rubino and his colleagues drew on health records from more than 800,000 people in the UK, US, China and Spain to test a diagnostic approach for obesity that he and other world experts proposed last year in a Lancet Commission report . They used the records to track people’s health for up to 15 years.
Under the new definition, someone with a BMI over 40 is considered obese, but doctors check people with a lower BMI for excess body fat by looking at their waist measurement.
A BMI of 30-plus with a raised waist measurement or waist-to-height ratio counts as obese, as does a BMI from 25 to 29.9 if waist measurement and waist-to-height ratio are high. In most countries, a raised waist measurement means more than 102cm (40in) for men and 88cm for women, while thresholds for a high waist-to-height ratio are about 0.57.
In a second step of the diagnosis, doctors distinguish between clinical obesity, meaning an active disease where excess body fat is already impairing organ function, and pre-clinical obesity, where the extra fat is a health risk but has yet to cause problems.

That’s how Professor Daniel Mège described the discovery of trace volcanic gases on Mars that could be key to finding life on the Red Planet.
The discovery centers around hydrogen chloride gas seeping out through volcanic rifts—something of a “smoking gun” that suggests Mars is not geologically dead, but merely sleeping.
These gases hint at magma, which, when coming into contact with groundwater can produce warm habitable niches for organisms beneath the Red Planet’s surface.
“If hydrothermal systems are active, they could contain the ingredients and energy needed for microorganisms to develop, and shield microorganisms from the hostile and changing environment above the surface,” one of the scientists behind the discovery hypothesized.
Mars is studded with the largest volcanoes in the solar system, and fresh fissures on the surface of one of the largest, called Alba Mons, hint at volcanically active spots under the surface.

Evidence for active volcanism on Mars has always been extremely elusive, yet enough has been identified in the form of geologically-recent lava flows and “marsquakes” over the last 50 years, so as never to rule it out.

items.text:
Octopuses are talented escape artists, capable of squeezing their bodies through seemingly impenetrable gaps to avoid danger, find hidden prey or break out of captivity . Scientists have long wondered how these eight-limbed creatures manage such impressive feats of flexibility. Now, they say they have some answers.
A study published November 5 in the Journal of Experimental Biology describes the step-by-step processes some octopuses use to cram themselves into tight spaces. In addition to expanding our understanding of these crafty cephalopods, the findings could help engineers improve the design of soft robots that need to fit into small spaces, such as those used during search-and-rescue missions.
“You always just think as a biologist that this is a minor question: How to squeeze your body into a crevice, through a hole or into a cave,” study co-author Michael Kuba , a biologist at the University of Naples Federico II in Italy, tells IFLScience ’s Rachael Funnell. “But working with soft robotic engineers, you realize that there is so much more to how they manage to do this. They have several steps of the movement, and they have specific postures and body parts they use to move through a hole.”
In the study, Kuba and colleagues conducted laboratory experiments involving three subadult common octopuses ( Octopus vulgaris ) and four juvenile Mayan octopuses ( O. maya ). The team started by measuring the distance between each animal’s eyes to determine the size of the semi-rigid cartilage casing surrounding their brains. Then, they adjusted a clear, acrylic tank partition to create a single, central hole that was either smaller or larger than the measurements, which ranged from about 0.4 to 1.4 inches. One at a time, they placed the octopuses in the tank, then watched and filmed what happened next.

Octopus bodies are mostly soft and pliable. These creatures have only two stiffer body parts: a cartilaginous shell that protects their brains and a beak —made of a hard material called chitin—that they use to eat.

items.text:
No wonder we need to seek out these kinds of posts. Nowadays, we can get the news at our fingertips, and more than ever, we're fully aware of the major geopolitical and social crises happening not only in our own countries but also around the world .
In a way, being informed is good. But it can also become overwhelming. According to the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism, around 40% of people globally report actively avoiding the news at times for a variety of reasons. Many cite exhaustion, depression, and even a sense of powerlessness caused by the constant coverage of conflict, economic struggles, and war.
And unfortunately, we're almost wired to focus on the negative. While these posts are undeniably wholesome and meant to bring out positive feelings, psychologists point out that humans have what is known as a “negativity bias.”
This means our brains are naturally wired to scan for threats and danger. And now that we live in an era of algorithm-driven infinite feeds, we're constantly bombarded with all kinds of content whenever we're staring at a screen . This can lead to chronic stress, making the consumption of positive content feel like a necessary psychological antidote.
Animals are just one example of what makes us feel good. Not only are they fluffy, innocent, and adorably goofy, but there's also a deeper reason we feel calmer when we look at many of these images.
It all comes down to what Austrian ethologist and Nobel laureate Konrad Lorenz called “Kindchenschema,” or baby schema. He observed that physical traits such as disproportionately large heads, high foreheads, big eyes, and rounded bodies often trigger an innate and involuntary caregiving response in humans. And that's exactly why kitties and puppies tug at our heartstrings.

And that's hardly the only research conducted on the power of cute things. Dr. Jessica Fall-Myrick surveyed 7,000 internet users about their consumption of cute animal content online, and the findings suggest it can have real benefits for our brains.
Participants who viewed cute animal content reported higher energy levels and more positive emotions overall. It also helped reduce negative emotions such as anxiety, sadness, and guilt. Ultimately, the study describes viewing animal content online as an accessible form of digital emotion regulation — a modern-day happy pill.

Other methods to combat invasive species have been costly and time-consuming, and the lack of effective early-detection methods has limited ecologists’ ability to control further colonization by invasive species.
Dr. Annegret Grimm-Seyfarth and her colleagues at the Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research (UFZ) tested the feasibility of a volunteer dog-handler training program, so citizen scientists could join the fight.
31 dogs and their owners were trained between 2021 and 2023 using three highly problematic invasive plant species: Himalayan balsam, common ragweed, and those in the knotweed family, such as Japanese knotweed ( Fallopia spp. complex, Impatiens glandulifera, and Ambrosia artemisiifolia ).

items.text:
For generations, human cannibalism in prehistoric Europe was viewed as a desperate response to starvation. Now, a forensic re-examination of three prehistoric cave sites in southern Spain reveals that people ate human remains as a ritual for millennia, including after violent clashes or as a standard funeral rite.
Researchers analyzed 967 skeletal fragments representing at least 60 individuals recovered from the caves of Malalmuerzo , Carigüela and Majolicas in the province of Granada . Using high-resolution microscopy, machine learning and radiocarbon dating, the team discovered that these grisly feasts were not confined to a single crisis, such as war or starvation. Instead, they unfolded in “context-dependent episodes” between roughly 5300 B.C.E. and 3760 B.C.E., according to a recent study published in the Journal of Archaeological Science .
The bone assemblages were first excavated in the 1970s under the direction of Miguel C. Botella , a forensic anthropologist at the University of Granada. Fifty years later, Botella joined a multi-disciplinary team to subject the historical collection to modern forensic analysis.
“Returning to these materials with new tools has allowed us to address questions that were impossible to answer at the time,” lead author Palmira Saladié , an archaeologist at the Catalan Institute of Human Paleoecology and Social Evolution, explains in a statement .
By scrutinizing butchery traces, impact fractures and tooth marks under the microscope, the researchers distinguished between injuries inflicted on fresh bone around the time of death and natural degradation that took place years later. The story begins with the younger cousin of New Jersey high schooler Shashank Madala, who would on occasion get upset at family gatherings. The adults who loved him most would gather around and guess out loud about whether he was hungry or whether the room was too loud.
They were often wrong, Madala writes, and over time the boy stopped trying to tell them. Madala was just 15, with a single computer science class behind him, but nevertheless decided to take action.
Madala’s early versions of Kora gave caregivers one fast, confident answer, and he came to see that this repeated the very mistake his family had made with his cousin. He rebuilt the app to slow adults down, offering more than one possible reading and surfacing what it is least sure about.
The philosophy behind his work was that technology aimed at autistic children is often built to change the child. His aim was to flip that script.
“A tool that announces that a child is angry invites the adult to stop looking at the child,” he wrote in Autism Spectrum News in August.
A caregiver points a phone camera at the child, and Kora offers several possible readings of what the child may be feeling, with bars for happy, sad, angry, afraid, and neutral, along with suggestions for how to respond.
In a display of responsible use of AI beyond his years, Madala also programmed Kora to now flag when it is unsure, leaving the final judgment to the adult who knows the child.

Now a team of neurologists in the US trialling a novel form of immunotherapy have reported “exciting” and “very encouraging” results: the treatment has prompted dramatic improvements in people living with SPS.
Patients who previously needed help with basic daily tasks and struggled to walk have regained their ability to take part in everyday life, with some even returning to work and resuming hobbies, according to doctors at the Mayo Clinic.

Neurologists said the results, published in medical journal Jama Neurology, were particularly exciting because patients had been able to return to activities they feared they would never be able to return to.
Dr Anastasia Zekeridou, a neurologist and researcher at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, said: “What was most striking was the degree of improvement we saw in some patients.
“With existing treatments, we may be able to improve symptoms but we very rarely see patients return to their previous level of function. These early results are very encouraging and the key question now is whether those improvements will be sustained over time.”

A merchant marine cadet has been hailed as a hero for saving a father who nearly drowned in a swimming pool while trying to save his drowning 25-year-old son.
“When I arrived at the pool, I saw the father floating face down,” Zion Jerge said , recounting the rescue that took place near his home in Foster City, California.
He had first heard screams, and ran towards an apartment complex where he saw scenes of obvious distress around a pool behind a fence.
“My body kind of just took over, like a fight-or-flight reaction, and I jumped over the fence and into the pool. I pulled the father out first because he was the one I saw first.”
“After I pulled him out, I heard more screaming and realized there was another man lying at the bottom of the deep end, which was his son he was trying to save. Once I pulled the son out of the pool, I realized he was unconscious.”
The California Polytechnic State University Marine Academy cadet immediately began CPR on the son. After expelling water from his lungs, he was again breathing on his own.
Foster City Police Department officers and San Mateo Consolidated Fire Department personnel arrived when Jerge’s work was finished. The man’s 25-year-old son was conscious and accompanied paramedics to the hospital for further examination and recovery.

GLP-1 products such as Ozempic and Mounjaro spread but many in poorer countries struggle to get basic diabetes treatment
The gold rush into GLP-1 weight-loss drugs risks diverting pharmaceutical firms’ attention away from diabetes treatments such as insulin, the head of the Access to Medicine Foundation has warned.
GLP-1 blockbuster medications such as Novo Nordisk’s Ozempic and Eli Lilly’s Mounjaro have revolutionised obesity and diabetes treatment but there has been a greater focus by companies on weight loss, according to a report from the Netherlands-based non-profit group.
The group warned that many people cannot even get hold of basic insulin, critical for people with type 1 diabetes, and many countries were struggling to access GLP-1 medications at all – as the explosion in their popularity continues since the weight-loss jab Wegovy launched in 2021.
Diabetes affects an estimated 589 million adults globally, 81% of whom live in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) such as Pakistan, Egypt and Jordan.
“A lot of the GLP-1 drugs are just starting to enter these LMIC markets for obesity,” said Jay Iyer, the foundation’s chief executive, adding: “You have a lot of attention on GLP-1s, but a lot of it is directed towards the obesity market, and that’s not going to help people with type 1 diabetes who after 105 years of insulin development still do not have access to the drug.”
Companies are able to charge far higher prices and enjoy greater profit margins on weight-loss injections and pills , compared with other medication such as insulin.
“There is a risk that any of the three – Sanofi, [Eli] Lilly or Novo [Nordisk]– could leave the insulin market, and that will be disastrous for supply to insulin especially for people living with type 1 diabetes and insulin-dependent type 2 diabetes,” Iyer said.
Denmark’s Novo Nordisk has announced plans to phase out some of its older diabetes products, including insulin pens. However, Sanofi has just broken ground on a new insulin production site at its BioCampus in Frankfurt. The French company supplies insulin to 15 million people in more than 100 countries each year. Eli Lilly received US approval for a new once-weekly insulin injection for adults with type 2 diabetes in September.
Novo said: “We will carefully review the index’s findings, including opportunities to broaden access to analogue insulins and extend access plans to more low- and middle-income countries.”
